tldr: This is a loose grouping of three independent arXiv papers on LLM agent memory, linked by topic rather than one event. It opened on Nov 3 with a paper on choosing which text memories to retrieve, then moved to memory for long-running character dialogue on Nov 12.
whats_new: A Nov 19 paper reports deployment lessons from agents that distill memory from their own history to avoid repeat procedural failures such as mis-paginating an API or resolving the wrong entity.
why_it_matters: Agent memory is shifting from one fixed retrieval step to a design choice about what to store and when to inject it, which affects context cost and repeat-failure rates.

beats.headline: Adaptive selection of extracted text memories
beats.summary: Frames production agent memory as a bottleneck built from text key points pulled out of over-limit context.

beats.headline: Mental-state-driven memory for long-term character dialogue
beats.summary: Argues passive semantic retrieval misses how shared history shapes a relationship.

beats.headline: Self-distilled memory targets recurring procedural failures
beats.summary: Agents learn from their own trajectories, and the paper asks how much they should keep.

open_questions: Does self-distilled memory reduce repeat failures on public long-horizon agent benchmarks, not just the authors' tasks?
At what memory size does retrieval start hurting answers instead of helping them?
Will any agent framework ship adaptive memory selection as a built-in option?
take_for_builders: Log your agent's recurring failures (pagination, entity resolution, unprompted answers) before adding a memory layer, so you can measure whether stored lessons actually reduce them.

day_captions.043490c38692d4af: Sets the starting problem: text memory extracted from overflow context is a retrieval bottleneck.
day_captions.f48f97340f1b60b5: Extends the theme from task agents to conversational memory that tracks evolving relationships.
day_captions.32373812989fabcd: Adds deployment evidence: memory learned from the agent's own history, aimed at named procedural failure modes.
